"Europe has money for defense. What it doesn't have is time."

An analysis by Tetiana Nikolaienko for Ukrainska Pravda brings together statements from senior European military commanders, defense officials, and policymakers at the 6th European Defense & Security Conference in Brussels.

Despite rising defense spending, Europe is struggling with slow weapons production, shortages of air defense systems, fragmented procurement, and insufficient cooperation between manufacturers.

EU countries spent €418 billion on defense in 2025, with spending expected to reach €454 billion in 2026. Yet only 24% of equipment is purchased through joint procurement, well below the 40% target for 2027. Major manufacturers have orders booked for an average of five years, and in some cases up to nine.

Here's what European officials said:

▪️ Alexander Mattelaer, defense policy director at Belgium's Ministry of Defense, raised concerns about Europe's limited stocks of interceptor missiles.

He questioned how many anti-ballistic missile interceptors European armies still have in reserve and what would happen if Putin turned Russia's growing production of Iskander and Oreshnik missiles against European cities.

▪️ General Frederik Vansina, Belgium's top military commander, highlighted the enormous cost of air defense, pointing out that Europe is using AMRAAM missiles costing around $2 million to shoot down Shahed drones worth approximately $20,000.

Without control of the skies, European cities could face the same bombardment as Ukrainian cities.

▪️ Joachim Sucker, Director of OCCAR's Executive Administration, warned that increased defense spending alone cannot solve Europe's problems.

"Funding alone does not deliver capabilities," he said.

Sucker recalled how Europe once had plenty of time but lacked money. Now it has money, but almost no time left.

Competing national requirements, complex regulations, and industrial interests continue to delay major defense projects.

▪️ Andrey Novakov, a Bulgarian Member of the European Parliament, criticized Europe's slow response to the growing drone threat and its failure to turn research and investment into practical technologies.

He pointed to drone incidents in Poland, Romania, Bulgaria, Estonia, and Lithuania, despite European promises to strengthen anti-drone defenses.

Ukraine can provide a crucial missing element in Europe's defense strategy: real battlefield experience, rapid technological innovation, and the ability to test and adapt weapons under actual combat conditions.

Five key areas where European and Ukrainian defense cooperation could make a difference:

▪️ Common priorities. Focusing on urgent gaps: missile defense, space-based intelligence and early warning, maritime surveillance in the Black and Baltic Seas, and critical infrastructure protection.

▪️ Flexible contracts. European manufacturers need long-term orders, but rapidly evolving military technology demands contracts that allow upgrades and adjustments rather than locking countries into potentially outdated solutions.

▪️ Direct battlefield feedback. Many technologies presented in Europe as innovations become ineffective within just 20 minutes of real combat.

▪️ Joint production and European components. Europe wants to reduce its dependence on inexpensive Chinese components and American systems and technologies, including AMRAAM, F-35, Starlink, and Palantir. Combining Ukrainian and European orders, expertise, and production capabilities could help develop competitive alternatives.

▪️ Trust and long-term partnerships. European companies are interested in Ukraine's battlefield experience and rapid procurement practices, but need better ways to connect with Ukrainian manufacturers.

The opportunity is not simply to support Ukraine, but to make Ukrainian defense expertise an integral part of Europe's future security system.

📹: Andrius Kubilius, European Commissioner for Defense and Space, at the European Business Summit 2026.
